cards.front: An {{c1::ecosystem}} is all the living things in an area and their nonliving surroundings.
cards.quote: ecosystem: all the living things in an area and their nonliving surroundings
cards.section: Explain: living and nonliving parts of an ecosystem

cards.front: What counts as a biotic factor in an ecosystem? Give two examples.
cards.back: A living or once-living part: organisms, their parts, and their wastes. Examples: a fallen leaf, a fish scale, osprey droppings, parasites, disease-causing germs.
cards.quote: A biotic factor is a living or once-living part: organisms, their parts, and their wastes.
cards.section: Explain: living and nonliving parts of an ecosystem

cards.front: Why can the deep water of the Chesapeake Bay have too few phytoplankton?
cards.back: Light fades as water gets deeper. Light is an abiotic factor, and deep down there is too little of it for plankton to make food from sunlight.
cards.why: Abiotic factors help decide what can live in a place.
cards.quote: Light fades as water gets deeper, so deep down there is too little light for the plankton that make food from sunlight.
cards.section: Explain: living and nonliving parts of an ecosystem

cards.front: Nearly every food web starts with a {{c1::producer}}, an organism that makes its own food.
cards.quote: Nearly every food web starts with a producer, an organism that makes its own food.
cards.section: Explain: food chains and food webs

cards.front: In a food chain, which way do the arrows point, and what do they show?
cards.back: From food to eater. They show the way the energy moves, so an arrow from menhaden to osprey means energy moves from menhaden to osprey.
cards.quote: its arrows point from food to eater, the way the energy moves
cards.section: Explain: food chains and food webs

cards.front: In the food chain sunlight → phytoplankton → zooplankton → menhaden → osprey, what order of consumer is the osprey?
cards.back: Third-order. Zooplankton eat producers (first-order), menhaden eat zooplankton (second-order), and ospreys eat menhaden (third-order).
cards.quote: A second-order consumer eats first-order consumers. A third-order consumer eats second-order consumers.
cards.section: Explain: food chains and food webs

cards.front: A larger fish eats menhaden. Is it a second-order or third-order consumer?
cards.back: It depends on the path. It is third-order on phytoplankton → zooplankton → menhaden → larger fish, and second-order on phytoplankton → menhaden → larger fish.
cards.why: Order depends on the path through the web, not only on the species.
cards.quote: The larger fish is third-order on the longer path and second-order on the shorter path.
cards.section: Explain: food chains and food webs

cards.front: What does a decomposer do in a food web? Name two kinds.
cards.back: It breaks down dead matter and wastes from every level. Many bacteria and fungi are decomposers.
cards.quote: such as many bacteria and fungi, break down dead matter and wastes from every level
cards.section: Explain: food chains and food webs

cards.front: A disease kills many menhaden in the Bay. Will only the ospreys be affected?
cards.back: No. Menhaden are linked to many organisms in a food web, so ospreys, larger fish, and plankton could all change.
cards.why: A food web links many chains.
cards.quote: So a disease that killed many menhaden could change ospreys, larger fish, and plankton.
cards.section: Explain: food chains and food webs

cards.front: At each feeding step, where does much of the energy in the food go?
cards.back: It is given off as thermal energy (heat) during life processes such as swimming and breaking down sugar in respiration.
cards.quote: Much of it is given off as thermal energy (heat) during life processes such as swimming and breaking down sugar in respiration
cards.section: Explain: why each level has less energy

cards.front: Plankton energy goes into a menhaden. Why does only some of it reach an osprey?
cards.back: Much becomes heat. Some food passes through undigested and goes to decomposers. Only the rest is built into the fish's body, and ospreys do not catch every menhaden.
cards.why: Menhaden that die uneaten also give their energy to decomposers.
cards.quote: Only the rest is built into the fish's body, where an osprey can get it.
cards.section: Explain: why each level has less energy

cards.front: As a rough rule, about {{c1::one-tenth}} of one level's energy is available to the next level.
cards.quote: The simulation used a rough rule: about one-tenth of one level's energy is available to the next.
cards.section: Explain: why each level has less energy

cards.front: Producers capture 10,000 made-up units of energy. If one-tenth passes at each step, how much reaches the third-order consumers?
cards.back: 10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10. The third-order consumers get 10 units, one-thousandth of the start.
cards.quote: One-tenth passes three times, so the top receives one-thousandth of the starting energy: 10 of 10,000 made-up units.
cards.section: Explore: build an energy pyramid

cards.front: Producers capture 10,000 made-up units. If only 5 percent passes at each step, about how much reaches the third-order consumers?
cards.back: 10,000 × 0.05 × 0.05 × 0.05 = 1.25 units, much less than the 10 units at 10 percent.
cards.quote: Lower the percent to 5 and watch the top bar shrink much more, then return to 10.
cards.section: Explore: build an energy pyramid

cards.front: In the energy pyramid model, the producers' energy doubles while the percent passed and the number of levels stay fixed. What happens to the top bar?
cards.back: It doubles. Every level gets the same fraction of twice as much.
cards.quote: It doubles. Every level gets the same fraction of twice as much.
cards.section: Explore: build an energy pyramid

cards.front: Is the energy that is lost as heat at each feeding step used up, and can producers use it again?
cards.back: It is not used up; it changes form. The heat spreads into water and air, and producers cannot turn it back into food.
cards.quote: Energy is not used up; it changes form, and much becomes heat that spreads into water and air.
cards.section: Explain: why each level has less energy

cards.front: Does the energy pyramid tell you exactly how many top predators an ecosystem has? Why or why not?
cards.back: No. Energy limits top predators but gives no exact count. One large tree can feed many insects, so energy is not a head count.
cards.why: The pyramid gives the direction of change, not a headcount.
cards.quote: But energy is not a head count: one large tree can feed many insects, so energy limits top predators without giving an exact number.
cards.section: Explain: why each level has less energy

cards.front: In most ecosystems, why can matter be used again by producers but energy cannot?
cards.back: Energy flows one way: in as sunlight and out as heat that producers cannot reuse. Decomposers return carbon and nutrients, so matter cycles.
cards.why: Energy lost as heat at each step is one reason the top level has the least energy available.
cards.quote: In most ecosystems, energy flows one way, in as sunlight and out as heat.
cards.section: Explain: why each level has less energy

cards.front: At Silver Springs, Florida, second-order consumers took in 383 and third-order consumers took in 21 kilocalories per square meter per year. What percent passed to the third-order level?
cards.back: 21 ÷ 383 × 100 = about 5.5 percent, about half of the rough one-tenth rule.
cards.quote: We calculated the percentages from his numbers, so small differences mean little.
cards.section: Elaborate: real energy numbers from a Florida spring

cards.front: At Silver Springs, decomposers took in 5,060 kilocalories per square meter per year, more than the 3,368 taken in by plant eaters. Where could that energy come from?
cards.back: Decomposers are a side branch fed by all levels. They get energy from dead matter and wastes of producers and every consumer level, not only from plant eaters.
cards.quote: Decomposers took in more energy than the plant eaters. Where could that energy come from?
cards.section: Elaborate: real energy numbers from a Florida spring

cards.front: In the mealworm investigation, why does the plan include containers of oat bran with no mealworms?
cards.back: They measure how much mass the bran loses by drying. That loss is then not counted as food eaten.
cards.quote: Bran can lose mass by drying. Containers without mealworms measure that loss, so drying is not counted as food eaten.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the mealworm investigation, the mealworms gain far less mass than the bran they ate. What does this show, and which idea from food webs does it match?
cards.back: Most of the food did not become new mealworm; respiration and waste account for much of the rest. It matches the rule that at each feeding step only part of the energy is available to the next level.
cards.quote: If the mealworms gain much less mass than the bran they ate, most of the food did not become new mealworm.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: At Silver Springs, producers captured 20,810 kilocalories per square meter per year and gave off 11,977 as heat in their own respiration. How much became new plant material?
cards.back: 20,810 − 11,977 = 8,833 kilocalories per square meter per year.
cards.quote: Plants and algae gave off 11,977 as heat in their own respiration, so only 8,833 became new plant material.
cards.section: Elaborate: real energy numbers from a Florida spring
